item.title: Drops for Nvidia, Anthropic and other AI stocks drag the U.S. market back down
item.description: HONG KONG — Global stocks were mixed Tuesday after a rally on Wall Street as Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia’s CEO. U.S. futures edged higher. Oil prices extended their losses, falling close to their ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower Tuesday after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent to its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks once again led the way and yanked the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.5 per cent. Stocks outside of AI held up much better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423 points, or 0.9 per cent. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ 401(k) accounts because AI companies have grown into Wall Street’s most influential stocks. While the surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO announced Monday does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it. At the same time, high interest rates make it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres. To be sure, AI stocks and the broader U.S. market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour. For now, at least, the momentum is back downward. Nvidia fell 5.9 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, tumbled 11.8 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 4.8 per cent. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5 per cent to drop below US$83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as US$115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype. Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected. Confidence jumped sharply for Democrats and independents following the midterm election results, according to the Conference Board. That narrowed the wide gap between them and Republicans, whose confidence fell slightly. The results echo a report from the University of Michigan released earlier in the month, which also showed a rise in overall sentiment following the midterm elections and a drop in oil prices from late October. Companies in industries across the economy, meanwhile, continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer. Dollar Tree climbed 11.2 per cent after reporting bigger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than they did in last year’s third quarter, and more of them came in than last year. Kohl’s rallied 19.5 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected. Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. That’s a big deal because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated. All told, the S&P 500 fell 36.08 points to 7,201.09. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 423.39 to 50,018.70, and the Nasdaq composite fell 356.02 to 23,733.54. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.93 per cent from 4.92 per cent late Monday after drifting up and down earlier in the day. Oil prices rose, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil climbed 2.4 per cent to US$88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report

item.title: Macklem says inflation forecast is lower, but oil price pressures are lingering
item.description: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast. The Bank of Canada said back in October that it saw inflation rising to 3.5 per cent by the end of the year as stubbornly high global oil prices threatened to put more pressure on consumers. Statistics Canada said inflation held steady at 3.1 per cent in October. High gas prices from war in the Middle East continued to be the biggest driver of inflation, but the agency said upward pressure was broad-based across groceries and clothing as well. Macklem suggested at a press conference in Toronto on Tuesday that recent relief at the gas pumps should mean inflation holds around those levels through the end of the year. “The inflation forecast is a bit lower. Those costs that built up over the previous eight months, they’re still there, but there’s a bit of edge (that’s) come off the inflation forecast,” he said. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent October as it warned gas prices were staying higher for longer than first expected and inflationary pressures could start to spread. Officials signalled at the time that they’d “proceed carefully,” but there could be a need for more rate hikes to come. Macklem also addressed the current inflation outlook in a speech to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday. While he acknowledged the recent climbdown in global benchmark oil prices, he said that wasn’t the only factor monetary policymakers were weighing. “So far, businesses have largely absorbed the higher production and transport costs. But historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to consumer prices in the year ahead. This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence,” he said in prepared remarks. CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld said in a note to clients on Tuesday that the governor seemed to be downplaying the disinflationary impact of falling oil prices. Shenfeld said Macklem’s focus on lingering inflation risks suggests the central bank could be gearing up to deliver a second consecutive rate hike at its next decision on Dec. 9. “There was no direct reference to the December meeting, but what was apparent was that the governor was going out of his way to not show any changes in his thinking from October whenever possible,” he said. Odds of a quarter-point hike from the Bank of Canada next month stood at 79 per cent as of Tuesday, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. That’s up from nearly 63 per cent on Monday. Macklem said Tuesday the Bank of Canada will be weighing next week’s releases of gross domestic product data for the third quarter and November labour market figures before deciding what to do at its final policy rate decision of the year. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

item.title: Bank of Canada keeps 2% inflation target but adjusts what to track
item.description: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there. The federal government and the Bank of Canada renewed the central bank’s five-year mandate earlier this month and maintained the target for two per cent annual inflation, as measured by Statistics Canada’s consumer price index, or CPI. The central bank maintains a one-to-three per cent band around that target, which offers some wiggle room to execute monetary policy. Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem spoke to a business crowd in Toronto on Tuesday where he hailed the two per cent target as a “clear and well-understood objective” since it was implemented in 1995. Anchoring its policy rate decisions on that inflation target helped the Bank of Canada tame the post-COVID surge in inflation, Macklem argued in prepared remarks. But he acknowledged that Canadians didn’t respond well to inflation and the rate hikes it necessitated. “For many Canadians, it was their first experience with high inflation. And they didn’t like it. As we reviewed our framework, we held consultations across the country to hear from Canadians. We heard a lot of anger,” Macklem said during a speech at the Economic Club of Canada on Tuesday. The head of the Bank of Canada acknowledged the central bank could have done a better job in the post-pandemic period, which saw inflation pressures compound after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Monetary policymakers were “too slow to recognize the persistence of inflationary pressures and how broadly they were spreading through the economy,” Macklem said. The Bank of Canada has updated its forecasting models to get a better handle on how supply shocks are likely to affect inflation and the economy, and whether monetary policy needs to intervene. Policymakers are also upping their communication efforts to get Canadians to go along with them on rate decisions. Macklem acknowledged Tuesday that Bank of Canada has spurred confusion in the past over how it discussed underlying price trends. The Bank of Canada previously downplayed its preferred measures of core inflation, CPI-trim and CPI-median, as it tried to gauge how supply shocks were affecting the economy. “We wanted to be transparent about where we saw inflation pressures and where we did not. But we weren’t as clear as we hoped,” Macklem said. “Canadians found it confusing when we discussed measures that strip out volatile prices such as food and gasoline. After all, these are important parts of the family budget. And financial market participants sometimes felt that we were moving the inflation goalposts.” Excluding the right measures can help give the Bank of Canada a clearer picture of inflation trends and cut through temporary forces pushing prices higher, Macklem said. Now, the Bank of Canada will put its focus back on an old measure called CPIX, which excludes eight fixed sets of items from the inflation calculation to provide a consistent benchmark of how prices are evolving. The Bank of Canada used CPIX to guide monetary policy decisions from 2001 to 2016. Some of the items excluded from CPIX are gasoline, mortgage interest costs and fruits and vegetables. Macklem helped develop CPIX as an indicator for the central bank 25 years ago. He told reporters after his speech Tuesday that the measure gives a more granular view of areas like food and energy by excluding the items most sensitive to temporary price fluctuations. The Bank of Canada will retain what’s called CPI-trim as its other core measure, which strips out the items seeing the most extreme price changes in each month. In tandem, the updated core inflation metrics give the Bank of Canada one view of a fixed basket of goods and services as well as one that adjusts based on what’s changing most rapidly. “I think that gives you a diversity; hopefully the best of both worlds,” Macklem said. The Bank of Canada will also start publishing an inflation dashboard on its website to show how various measures of price pressures are trending. Macklem was asked in an armchair discussion after his speech what indicators economists should look at if they want to better gauge the Bank of Canada’s interest rate path — aside from headline inflation. But the central bank governor laughed and brushed off the question. “My pet peeve is that markets tend to focus — over-focus — on one or two indicators,” he said. “We have a big, complex economy that is highly connected to the world. You can’t summarize it in one or two indicators.” Macklem explained that, while the Bank of Canada’s updated core metrics can help monetary policymakers see where prices are headed, keeping overall inflation at two per cent remains the central bank’s North Star. “Total CPI inflation is our target, and it will be front and centre in all our communications. Various indicators help us understand where inflation is headed and the risks around that forecast. But they are inputs to our analysis, not targets,” he said. In addition to shifting the core inflation metrics, the Bank of Canada’s new five-year mandate drops language from the previous statement about employment. The 2021 mandate included an agreement with the federal government that monetary policy ought to support “maximum sustainable employment” when possible — a reference that’s absent from the 2026 renewal. The new mandate also removed a previous allusion to the need to account for the impact of climate change on the Canadian economy and financial system. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

item.title: Oil and gas drillers optimistic heading into 2027, but warn of labour shortages
item.description: Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year, but labour shortfalls could threaten that momentum. Industry advocacy group Enserva has released its annual state of the industry report, which calls for an increase in the number of wells drilled in 2027 versus this year. But it flags competition for workers as a major challenge at a time when artificial intelligence data centres and major infrastructure projects draw from the same talent pool. Bradley Fedora, president and CEO of Trican Well Service Ltd., says the prospect of “hyperinflation” in the cost of labour and materials is what scares him most. Thomas Alford, president of completion and production services at Precision Drilling, told reporters at the event that it can take up to eight years to train up a competent drill rig staffer, and the industry has been so unstable in recent years that it’s been hard for those workers to get that consistent job experience. Gurpreet Lail, Enserva’s president and CEO, says the sector needs to work hard to attract and keep talent as data centre developments offer big paycheques to tradespeople and perks that have until now been “unheard of.” --- Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.
